explanations.explanation: Nice thought, friend, but that's not what the text says. It says Nadab "…did evil in the sight of the LORD and walked in the way of his father and in his sin, which he had caused Israel to commit." (1 Kings 15:26) So he doesn't break from Jeroboam's path, he follows it. Some people inherit a house, and Nadab inherited a habit.

That's right. Nadab, Jeroboam's son and king of Israel, does evil in the sight of the LORD. The text says he "…walked in the way of his father and in his sin, which he had caused Israel to commit." (1 Kings 15:26) No break, no fresh start, just the same road with a new king on it.

You got it, baker! Ahijah the Shilonite is the prophet the text names here, the one through whom the LORD spoke this word (1 Kings 15:29). When the LORD says something, it lands right where He said it would.

Good name, friend, but Nathan isn't the one here. Nathan was the prophet the LORD sent to David, Israel's king in the days before the kingdom split (2 Samuel 12:1). Here the text says the word came through "…His servant Ahijah the Shilonite…" (1 Kings 15:29) Nathan's story is a whole different shelf in the bakery.

Close, baker, you picked a real prophet! Gad was David's seer, and the word of the LORD came to him in David's days (2 Samuel 24:11). But this word about Jeroboam's house came through Ahijah the Shilonite (1 Kings 15:29). Right job title, different king's days.

explanations.answer: Jeroboam sinned and made Israel sin
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. The text says it was "…because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and had caused Israel to commit, and because he had provoked the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger." (1 Kings 15:30) Notice it isn't only his own sin. It's also the sin he caused Israel to commit.

explanations.answer: Jeroboam taxed the people too heavily
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd guess that, friend, kings and money go together like dough and a hot oven. But this passage never gives that as the reason. It says the house of Jeroboam ends "…because of the sins Jeroboam had committed and had caused Israel to commit…" (1 Kings 15:30)

explanations.answer: Jeroboam made a treaty with the Philistines
explanations.explanation: The Philistines do show up in this stretch, but only as the people of Gibbethon, the city under siege (1 Kings 15:27). Nobody makes a treaty with them here. The reason the text gives is that Jeroboam sinned, caused Israel to sin and provoked the LORD to anger (1 Kings 15:30).

That's it, baker. The text says, "…there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel throughout their days." (1 Kings 15:32) Two kingdoms, two kings, and no handshake in sight. Remember, this is the split that began back in 1 Kings 12:19-20.

I wish, friend, but the text says the opposite. "…there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel throughout their days." (1 Kings 15:32) The verse gives us war, not peace. And it says throughout their days, so this wasn't a short fight.

Trade sounds nice, like swapping cookie boxes across the border. But the text never mentions any trade between them. It says "…there was war between Asa and Baasha king of Israel throughout their days." (1 Kings 15:32)

explanations.answer: He raised him from nothing to be ruler
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! God says, "…I lifted you out of the dust and made you ruler over My people Israel…" (1 Kings 16:2) Dust is about as low as it gets, and God raised Baasha from there to the throne. That's what makes the rest of the verse so sharp.

explanations.answer: He helped him win his wars with Asa
explanations.explanation: The text does say there was war between Baasha and Asa (1 Kings 15:32). But it never says God helped Baasha win it, and that's not what God reminds him of. He says, "…I lifted you out of the dust and made you ruler over My people Israel…" (1 Kings 16:2)

explanations.answer: He gave him the city of Gibbethon
explanations.explanation: Gibbethon is the Philistine city where Nadab was besieging when Baasha struck him down (1 Kings 15:27). But God never says He gave Baasha that city. What He reminds Baasha of is this: "…I lifted you out of the dust and made you ruler over My people Israel…" (1 Kings 16:2)

You got it, baker. God says, "…I will make your house like that of Jeroboam son of Nebat…" (1 Kings 16:3) Baasha wiped out Jeroboam's house, and now his own gets the same ending. The path he copied leads to the same place.

Good name, friend, but it's not the one in the verse. David was Israel's king before Solomon (1 Kings 2:10-12). God says, "…I will make your house like that of Jeroboam son of Nebat…" (1 Kings 16:3) Baasha walked in Jeroboam's way, so Jeroboam's ending is the comparison.

Solomon was David's son and sat on his throne (1 Kings 2:12), before the kingdom split (1 Kings 12:19-20). But he's not the name in this verse. God says, "…I will make your house like that of Jeroboam son of Nebat…" (1 Kings 16:3) Same road Baasha walked, same ending named.

Yes, baker! Baasha was buried in Tirzah, the same city where he reigned (1 Kings 15:33, 16:6). That's where the throne sat during his twenty-four years. Tirzah keeps showing up in this passage, so keep it handy.
Right on! Baasha's son Elah reigned in his place (1 Kings 16:6). Elah is the next king in the line. Remember that name.
Bethel is where Jeroboam set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28-29). It's not where Baasha was buried. The text says he "…was buried in Tirzah…" (1 Kings 16:6)
Nadab was Jeroboam's son, the king Baasha struck down (1 Kings 15:27-28). He isn't Baasha's son. The son who reigns in Baasha's place is Elah (1 Kings 16:6).

Shechem doesn't show up anywhere in this passage, friend. The text says Baasha "…was buried in Tirzah…" and his son reigned in his place (1 Kings 16:6). When a name isn't in the verse, I just let it sit on the cooling rack.

That's right, baker. The text says the word came "…because of all the evil he had done in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger with the work of his hands and becoming like the house of Jeroboam, and also because Baasha had struck down the house of Jeroboam." (1 Kings 16:7) So striking down Jeroboam's house is one of the reasons listed. It's right there in the sum-up.

Look closely, friend, because it's in there. The text says the word came against Baasha "…because of all the evil he had done in the sight of the LORD…" and "…also because Baasha had struck down the house of Jeroboam." (1 Kings 16:7) That's one reason it lists. So the statement is true.

explanations.answer: Zimri commander of half his chariots
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Zimri was Elah's servant and the commander of half his chariots (1 Kings 16:9). The text says he conspired against Elah while Elah was in Tirzah getting drunk at Arza's house. Then Zimri struck Elah down and reigned in his place (1 Kings 16:10).

explanations.answer: Arza the steward of his household
explanations.explanation: Arza is the host here, friend. Elah was getting drunk in his house, and Arza is called the steward of Elah's household (1 Kings 16:9). But the text names someone else as the one who conspired. It's "…Elah’s servant Zimri, the commander of half his chariots…"

Joab was commander of David's army, in David's days (2 Samuel 8:16). That's a different king and a different time. Here the one who conspires is Zimri, commander of half of Elah's chariots (1 Kings 16:9).

You got it, baker! Jehu the prophet, the son of Hanani, is the one the LORD spoke through against Baasha (1 Kings 16:1, 12). It's the same word we heard earlier, now coming true. Zimri carries it out.

Elijah the Tishbite is a prophet who steps onto the scene at 1 Kings 17:1, but not yet here. This word was spoken against Baasha through Jehu the prophet (1 Kings 16:12). Hold onto Elijah's name, because you'll meet him later.

Samuel was a prophet from earlier days, the one who anointed Saul (1 Samuel 10:1). He isn't the one in this verse, friend. The text says the word was spoken "…against Baasha through Jehu the prophet." (1 Kings 16:12)

Careful, friend, the text says something different. It says this happened "…because of all the sins Baasha and his son Elah had committed and had caused Israel to commit…" (1 Kings 16:13) So Elah's sins are named right alongside his father's. It's not Baasha alone.

Right, baker. The text says it was "…because of all the sins Baasha and his son Elah had committed and had caused Israel to commit, provoking the LORD, the God of Israel, to anger with their worthless idols." (1 Kings 16:13) Both father and son are named. Elah wasn't just standing by.
Perfect, baker. The text says Zimri "…reigned in Tirzah for seven days." (1 Kings 16:15) A week is all he gets. That's a shorter run than most of my cookie batches.
Forty days is a nice round number, friend, but it's not this one. The text says Zimri "…reigned in Tirzah for seven days." (1 Kings 16:15) Seven is all he gets.

Ninety days would be a whole season, baker, and Zimri doesn't get anywhere near that. The text says he "…reigned in Tirzah for seven days." (1 Kings 16:15) It's a very short reign, and it's all in one verse.

explanations.answer: Proclaim Omri the army commander king
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The people in the camp heard that Zimri had conspired against the king and struck him down. Then "…there in the camp that very day, all Israel proclaimed Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel." (1 Kings 16:16) The troops act that same day. They make their own commander the king.

explanations.answer: Swear their loyalty to King Zimri
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other way, friend. The people in the camp heard that Zimri had conspired against the king and struck him down. Then "…all Israel proclaimed Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel." (1 Kings 16:16)

explanations.answer: Go home to their own tribes
explanations.explanation: They don't head home, baker. The text says they stayed right there and "…all Israel proclaimed Omri, the commander of the army, king over Israel." (1 Kings 16:16) Then Omri and all the Israelites marched up from Gibbethon (1 Kings 16:17). The army stays together and gets a new king.

That's right, baker. The text says Zimri died "…because of the sins he had committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD and following the example of Jeroboam and the sin he had committed and had caused Israel to commit." (1 Kings 16:19) Jeroboam's example shows up again. It keeps showing up in this passage.

I'd flip that one, friend. The text says Zimri died "…because of the sins he had committed, doing evil in the sight of the LORD and following the example of Jeroboam…" (1 Kings 16:19) So the statement is true. Jeroboam's name keeps coming up like a bad recipe.

explanations.answer: Omri's side wins and he becomes king
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! "…the followers of Omri proved stronger than those of Tibni son of Ginath. So Tibni died and Omri became king." (1 Kings 16:22) Half the people backed each man, and Omri's side came out stronger. Then Omri takes the throne.

explanations.answer: Tibni and Omri share the throne
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give us a shared throne, friend. It says "…the followers of Omri proved stronger than those of Tibni son of Ginath. So Tibni died and Omri became king." (1 Kings 16:22) One king, one throne.

explanations.answer: Tibni's side wins and Omri flees
explanations.explanation: Other way around, baker. The text says "…the followers of Omri proved stronger than those of Tibni son of Ginath." (1 Kings 16:22) Tibni died, and Omri became king. Nobody flees in this verse.

Perfect, baker! Omri bought the hill from Shemer for two talents of silver and built a city there, "…calling it Samaria after the name of Shemer, who had owned the hill." (1 Kings 16:24) The city is named for the man who owned the hill. Samaria will matter for the rest of this passage.

Shiloh is a real place in Scripture. Ahijah the Shilonite is named in this passage, and that name points to Shiloh (1 Kings 15:29). But Omri's city isn't called that. The text says he called it "…Samaria after the name of Shemer…" (1 Kings 16:24)

Hebron doesn't show up in this passage, friend. The text says Omri built a city on the hill he bought, "…calling it Samaria after the name of Shemer, who had owned the hill." (1 Kings 16:24) The name comes from the man who sold the land.

A brand new city doesn't change the record, friend. The text says, "…Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD and acted more wickedly than all who were before him." (1 Kings 16:25) So he doesn't do better than the kings before him. He does worse than all of them.

That's right, baker. "…Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD and acted more wickedly than all who were before him." (1 Kings 16:25) The next verse says he walked in all the ways of Jeroboam son of Nebat and in his sins (1 Kings 16:26). The city is new, but the way he walks isn't.

explanations.answer: He does more evil than all of them
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text says, "…Ahab son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him." (1 Kings 16:30) That includes his own father, who had already acted more wickedly than those before him (1 Kings 16:25). The bar keeps going up, and so does the evil.

explanations.answer: He does better than his father did
explanations.explanation: I get the hope, friend, but the text says otherwise. Omri acted more wickedly than all who were before him (1 Kings 16:25). Then Ahab "…did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him." (1 Kings 16:30) So he doesn't do better than his father.

explanations.answer: He does right in the LORD's eyes
explanations.explanation: Not in this passage, baker. The text says, "…Ahab son of Omri did evil in the sight of the LORD, more than all who were before him." (1 Kings 16:30) He isn't just a little off. He's worse than every king before him.
Yes, baker. The text says Ahab "…proceeded to serve and worship Baal." (1 Kings 16:31) Baal is a false god. The next verse says Ahab set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built.
Dagon is a false god of the Philistines (1 Samuel 5:2). But he isn't the one in this verse, friend. The text says Ahab "…proceeded to serve and worship Baal." (1 Kings 16:31)
Molech is a false god too, called the abomination of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:7). But he isn't who Ahab serves here. The text says Ahab "…proceeded to serve and worship Baal." (1 Kings 16:31)

You got it, baker. The text says, "…Ahab set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built in Samaria." (1 Kings 16:32) Ahab didn't just join in. He had built a temple for Baal, and it was in Samaria.

A tower is a fine thing to build, friend, but it's not in this verse. The text says, "…Ahab set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built in Samaria." (1 Kings 16:32) The temple came first, and the altar went inside.

A fortress would sound serious, baker, but that's not what the text says. Ahab "…set up an altar for Baal in the temple of Baal that he had built in Samaria." (1 Kings 16:32) The word is temple, and he had built it in Samaria.

That's it, baker. "Then he set up an Asherah pole." (1 Kings 16:33) First the altar for Baal, then the Asherah pole. The text says that is how Ahab did more to provoke the LORD than all the kings of Israel before him.
A golden ephod shows up in Gideon's story, where he made one from gold (Judges 8:27). It isn't what Ahab sets up here, friend. The text says, "Then he set up an Asherah pole." (1 Kings 16:33)
The bronze serpent goes back to Moses, who made one in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9). That's not what Ahab sets up here, baker. The text says, "Then he set up an Asherah pole." (1 Kings 16:33)

explanations.answer: His firstborn son and his youngest son
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker, and I think this one hurts. The text says, "At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he set up its gates…" (1 Kings 16:34) The cost was his sons. It's a heavy verse, and I won't make light of it.

explanations.answer: All the silver and gold he owned
explanations.explanation: Silver and gold aren't mentioned in the verse, friend. The text says the cost was his sons: "At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he set up its gates…" (1 Kings 16:34) It's a heavy one.

explanations.answer: His house and his fields in Bethel
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a house or fields, baker. Hiel the Bethelite paid with his sons: "At the cost of Abiram his firstborn he laid its foundation, and at the cost of Segub his youngest he set up its gates…" (1 Kings 16:34) I think this one is a hard verse to read.

That's right, baker. The text says it happened "…according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Joshua son of Nun." (1 Kings 16:34) Joshua spoke that word about Jericho long before, when he said whoever rebuilds the city will do it at the cost of his firstborn and his youngest (Joshua 6:26). It's a hard verse, but the text ties it to that word.

The text says otherwise, friend. It says this happened "…according to the word that the LORD had spoken through Joshua son of Nun." (1 Kings 16:34) Joshua, Israel's leader after Moses (Joshua 1:1-2), had spoken about rebuilding Jericho at the cost of a man's firstborn and youngest (Joshua 6:26). So the statement is true. It's a heavy verse, and the text ties it to that earlier word.
